articles.text: Night before last, in Miles City, the whole post-office block was destroyed by fire.
articles.summary: The post-office block in Miles City was destroyed by fire.

articles.text: The improvement in General Grant's condition goes steadily on and now it is confidently expected that he will live long enough to finish his war history.
articles.summary: General Grant's condition is improving and he is expected to finish his war history.

articles.text: Sorrowfully do we chronicle the fact that the war feeling between England and Russia is subsiding and that the two nations are now resorting to arbitration, Emperor Wilhelm, of Germany, has been appointed arbitrator.
articles.summary: The paper wryly regrets that the England-Russia war fever is subsiding into arbitration under Emperor Wilhelm.

articles.text: There is really no news of the Riel rebellion, except that the revolutionists seem to be strengthening constantly and the Dominion troops are either under command of an inefficient general or he is badly handicapped by the government officials. The only just and sensible way for the Dominion to settle this matter is to grant the half-breeds every one of their demands.
articles.summary: The paper says the Riel rebellion should be settled by granting the half-breeds' demands.

articles.text: Butte City is determined to make herself notorious. A bill has been prepared and doubtless by this time passed by the city council providing that the law prohibiting prize-fighting in Montana, should be inoperative June 16, the date set for the Sullivan-Ryan fight. Butte could be in far better business than to encourage such an exhibition. The worst of the matter is that by this measure Butte will take all the odium and receive not a penny's worth of benefit. It is almost a foregone conclusion that the fight will never take place.
articles.summary: The paper criticizes Butte for suspending the prize-fight law for the Sullivan-Ryan fight on June 16.

articles.text: The Belfield Courier, Vol 1, No. 1, is lying on our table. Louis C. Hay and Geo. Auld are editors and it is published by the Mandan Times. This latter fact is not mentioned editorially, but the earmarks of Bro. Cates' skill as a printer are as plainly manifest as is the idiocy of trying to get up a boom for a town by the aid of a paper which advertises its own inability to live otherwise than as a boom issue. It is a wonderfully short-sighted piece of folly for the boomers not to see that all will soon learn that the Courier is not printed in Belfield and then indeed will it prove a boomerang. We have the utmost good wishes for the future of Belfield but we have often expressed our views of the utter foolishness of booming a town. In this intance, however, the reason is plainly manifest. It is the last dying effort to squeeze a little juice out of a lemon that was picked too soon to ever contain any juice. If carefully nourished, the Courier may last two months, but we doubt it.
articles.summary: The paper mocks the first issue of the Belfield Courier, edited by Louis C. Hay and Geo. Auld and printed by the Mandan Times, as a town-boom sheet.

articles.headline: STOCK NOTES. Strayed or Stolen.
articles.text: From Little Missouri, July 6, 1884, a bay horse, eight years old and weighing about 1,000 pounds. The horse was branded with an anchor on left cheek and a hat brand on left shoulder. On the left hip he had a Texas brand, looking something like 7N, connected with flourish at top of N. A reward of $25 will be paid for information leading to his recovery. The horse is the property of John Pohl, and information can be brought or sent to the Cow Boy office.
articles.summary: Notice offering $25 reward for John Pohl's bay horse, strayed or stolen from Little Missouri on July 6, 1884.

articles.text:
Below are the three round-up districts in which our cowmen are interested. They will be kept standing until they begin. It will be noticed that the Powder river round-up begins May 7 and the Yellowstone and Little Missouri begin May 25:

ROUND-UP DISTRCT NO. 5.

Beginning at the mouth of Powder river, May 7, 1885; thence working down the Yellowstone river on the south side to the mouth of O'Fallon creek; thence up O'Fallon creek and its tributaries to its head; thence across to the head of Little Beaver; thence down Little Beaver to within ten miles of its mouth: thence across to the head of Big Beaver; thence down Big Beaver to the Northern Pacific railroad; thence across to the head of Glendive creek and down to the Yellowstone river; thence up the Yellowstone river including Cedar creek to the mouth of Cabin creek; thence up Cabin creek to its head. J. H. Lander, foreman.

ROUND-UP DISTRICT NO. 6.

Beginning at the mouth of Box Elder, May 25, 1885; thence working down the Little Missouri and its tributaries to a point about twenty miles below the mouth of Big Beaver; thence up Big Beaver and its tributaries to the Northern Pacific railroad. W. P. Osterhout, foreman.

ROUND-UP DISTRICT NO. 7.

Beginning May 25, 1885, at the mouth of the Yellowstone river, thence working up the Yellowstone river and tributaries on the east side to Glendive and the Northern Pacific railroad. R. H. Moore, foreman.
articles.summary: Boundaries, start dates and foremen of round-up districts 5, 6 and 7; the Powder river round-up begins May 7 and the Little Missouri and Yellowstone round-ups May 25.

articles.text: Senators Dawes and Ingalls, sub-committee of the senate committee on Indian affairs, will visit the Indian Territory soon and will either make a report making the closing of the Oklahoma country legitimate or prohibiting it altogether.
articles.summary: Senators Dawes and Ingalls will visit Indian Territory to report on the Oklahoma country.

articles.text: State veterinarian Paraan, of Illinois, reports that it is extremely difficult to stamp out pleuro-pneumonia as the local authorities manifest the greatest indifference in aiding him. The rooting out of contagious cattle diseases is a matter that should be taken entirely out of the hands of local authorities and placed in that of state and national officials. In this way only can contagious diseases be kept from spreading.
articles.summary: The paper argues that stamping out pleuro-pneumonia should be taken from local authorities and given to state and national officials.

articles.text: Four trotting horses have been recently purchased in this country by a gentleman from Vienna, Austria, and will be taken home by him for the purpose of starting a stable of this class of horses. A mile track has been established in that city, and racing will be instituted there during the coming summer upon the American plan.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Reprint from the N. W. L. S. Journal on a Viennese buyer of American trotting horses.

articles.text: And now, to still further dispel the illusion that Texas fever is only a scare, gotten up by northwestern cattlemen to to keep their ranges from being overstocked, the stockgrowers north of the Texas Pacific in Texas have quarantined against all cattle south of the road. This is liable to lead to serious difficulty among Texans, but the fact of the quarantine goes a long way toward proving that there is such a thing as Texas fever. In any event, it more firmly establishes the positions of the many states and territories which have recently quarantined against Texas cattle.
articles.summary: Stockgrowers north of the Texas Pacific have quarantined against cattle south of the road, which the paper says proves Texas fever is real.

articles.text: Cattle on the range are said to be in tip-top condition for this season of the year, and a large calf crop is anticipated. However it is not to be understood that they are beef fat, for that day has past, or that there are not a great many that are quite thin; but what we mean by tip-top condition is that they are in good living fix and thriving. Calves dropped now will find their mothers strong, and the range being good, will supply them with plenty of milk and the loss will be nominal. True, calves dropped out of season had a tough time of it, but it is safe to calculate on raising 95 per cent of those dropped since March 1st is, of course too early for calves to come. May 1st would be early enough if cattle men could regulate this as handily as sheep growers do. But this being an exceptional year the March crop fared well. And if the branding does not turn out well, owners will know the reason why and may conclude that the day of big calf crops like many other good things has passed and will return no more until cattle men learn, like sheep men, to control the breeding season.—[Rocky Mountain Husbandman.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Rocky Mountain Husbandman: range cattle are in good condition and a large calf crop is expected.

articles.text: The secretary of the Interior, according to instructions of the Montana association, has been earnestly petitioned by the president and secretary of the association, to see that the Montana Indians are properly cared for. Almost all the difficulty ever had with the Indians was due to the fact that the government promised to provide for them and then, through Indians agents, almost starved them, forcing them in many instances to eat their horses and dogs. In other words, although the intention of the government was good, the Indians have experienced a perfectly unreliable policy, being promised things that were never fulfilled. It is easy then to see how so many difficulties have arisen with the Indians. Smarting under a sense of wrong, they have tried, in their own way, to right it. We are not over-friendly to the Indians but we are more an enemy to the policy the government has adopted toward them and still more an enemy to the miserably ineffectual way the government has of carrying out its policy. By all means let us have a change. Anything will be an improvement over the present system.
articles.summary: The Montana stock association has petitioned the Secretary of the Interior to see that Montana Indians are cared for; the paper attacks government Indian policy.

articles.headline: Additional Local.
articles.text: Duck and geese are becoming plentiful on the river.
articles.summary: Ducks and geese are becoming plentiful on the river.

articles.text: The work of filling the new cold-storage rooms with ice is nearly completed.
articles.summary: The new cold-storage rooms are nearly filled with ice.

articles.text: A well, to be used for fire purposos has been built south of the Co's. offices.
articles.summary: A well for fire purposes has been built south of the Co.'s offices.

articles.text: A tight corrall for pigs is being built at the foot of the butte north-east of the slaughter-house.
articles.summary: A pig corral is being built near the slaughter-house.

articles.text: There will be a mile race at the rink Saturday night between George Bicknell and Pete Campbell.
articles.summary: A mile race at the rink Saturday night between George Bicknell and Pete Campbell is announced.

articles.text: "Max" has again gone home for a visit of a week or two. J. M. Stickel takes his place temporarily.
articles.summary: "Max" has gone home for a visit; J. M. Stickel takes his place.

articles.text: Considerable grading has been done lately and much more will be done soon. It materially improves the appearance of our streets.
articles.summary: Street grading has been done and more is planned.

articles.text: Many train-loads of gravel have been brought in to the slaughter-house side-track and the track will be raised several feet.
articles.summary: Train-loads of gravel have been brought to raise the slaughter-house side-track.

articles.text: The Hash-knife outfit was to begin gathering fat cattle for the Co., April 15. The first bunch can be expected here before June 1.
articles.summary: The Hash-knife outfit was to begin gathering fat cattle for the Co. April 15; first bunch expected before June 1.

articles.text: Grass never received a better start here than it has this spring. It is now long and old enough so that cattle will begin to pick up rapidly.
articles.summary: Grass has had an excellent start this spring.

articles.text: Everyone should remember the meeting at the rink to-morrow night and attend it with the intention of doing his individual best for the points brought up.
articles.summary: Readers are reminded of the meeting at the rink to-morrow night.

articles.text: "Otto von Bismarck" descended upon us yesterday and has now firmly convinced everyone that Franz Falk's beer is the elixir of life.
articles.summary: "Otto von Bismarck" arrived yesterday, promoting Franz Falk's beer.

articles.text: Hereafter, we will publish a weekly weather report by Mr. Martin and give the summary monthly. From many sources we have received complimentary notice of the faithful record kept by him.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy will publish a weekly weather report by Mr. Martin with a monthly summary.

articles.text: Large lodging houses will soon be built on the vacant lots north of the hotel for the accommodation of the Co's, men. It is also to be hoped that the Co. will build more dwelling houses, as there is pressing need for them.
articles.summary: Large lodging houses for the Co.'s men will be built north of the hotel.

articles.text: We have heard of several remarkable case of absent-mindedness, but the climax was capped Tuesday by Vic. Smith, who got so interested shooting flies off a log that he didn't notice that his bullets were going straight into the freight house, until his fire was returned.
articles.summary: Vic Smith, shooting flies off a log Tuesday, sent bullets into the freight house until his fire was returned.

articles.text: There is every probability that the stage line will be pulled off this week. Had the Hills merchants lived up to their promises, there could have been no difficulty in paying expenses. As it is, there is no use in benefitting people who will not return the compliment.
articles.summary: The stage line will probably be pulled off this week because Black Hills merchants did not keep their promises.

articles.text: As a result of the recent surveying work the lots on the south side of the track will be so arranged as to allow a side-track to be built near the bluff and extending to the brick-yard. The streets will also be changed so that the lots next the river will face that way. On this side the track, room will be made for a side-track next the butte and next to the right of way all the lots will be made to face the railroad. The Marquis will also try to secure the right of way from the railroad to turn it into a park.
articles.summary: Survey work will rearrange Medora lots and side-tracks; the Marquis will try to get the railroad right of way for a park.

articles.text: There has been some talk of appointing a deputy sheriff for Billings Co., to be under the Morton county sheriff. To this we wish to put in a desided negative for two reasons. First, it will put us more than ever under the dominion of Morton county and second, will do us but little more good than formerly as there will be no justice here before whom to swear out complaints. Instead of deputy sheriff we should have a deputy U. S. marshal.
articles.summary: The paper opposes a deputy sheriff for Billings county under the Morton county sheriff and wants a deputy U. S. marshal instead.

articles.text:
Howard Eaton came in from Belfield Tuesday evening, to which place he had ridden from Wadsworth's line camp at the head of Frank's creek and reported that a gun in the hands of Joe. Graham was accidentally discharged, shooting off his right middle finger and then the bullet went completely through the left thigh of Frank Wadsworth crushing the bone and making an ugly flesh wound in the right thigh. From what we could learn it will be necessary to amputate the leg, involving a serious operation. Dr. Roberts happened to be here and started immediately on horse-back for the scene of the accident.

[A later report brought in by Pierce Boland is that the leg was successfully amputated by Dr. Robarts and that the patient was doing as well as could be expected. At the time Pierce left the ball was still lodged in the right thigh.]
articles.summary: Howard Eaton reported that Joe Graham's gun accidentally went off at Wadsworth's line camp, wounding Frank Wadsworth, whose leg Dr. Roberts later amputated.

articles.headline: A Cowboy in a Sleeping Car.
articles.text:
"Where do I camp?" he inquired, and was shown a lower berth next to me.

"That's the pigeon hole, is it? All right, old son; just watch my motion while I file myself away."

At this juncture he was ordered to turn over his revolver to the porter, which he declined to do in a most prompt and spirited manner.

"Old Dad (his revolver) and me always sleep together, and we don't want no divorce," he explained.

The conductor remonstrated, but was advised not to try to "braid this mule's tail."

"This here's a sleepin' car, ain't it?" he at length inquired.

"Yes."

"Well, why in——don't you let people sleep, then, when they've paid and gone into your game? If you're aiming to keep people awake, and want company, just dance into the next car; there's lots of folks there that don't want to sleep, nohow, and 'll be glad to see you."

The conductor withdrew, and my friend pulled off his boots and stretched himself, with many comments, in an undertone, on the poverty of the surroundings.

In about ten minutes this erratic person had his head out in the aisle.

"Say! you boy,"—to the porter.

"Well, sah."

"Come a runnin'."

The porter drew near and was handed a pillow about as big as a pin cushion.

"Take that gooseha'r thing away," commanded the cowboy.

"Don't you want a pillow, sah?" asked the porter.

"That ain't no pillow, and I don't want it, nohow; I'm afraid it'll get in my ear."

After this, silence, and for a short time I slept. I roused up, however at an exclamation on the part of my neighbor.

"Hold on there, my son, jest drap them boots."

"I was only jest gwine to black 'em, boss."

"Drap 'em."

They drapped.

"Jest gwine to pull them spurs, I reckon. Now, don't monkey 'round my camp, takin' things, no more. If you want anythin' speak for it. If you can't speak make signs, and if you can't make signs, shake a bush. You hear me?"

"Yes, sah."

After this more silence. The wheels and rails again sang together, and the cars again kept approving time, and presently I slept without interruption.—[Northwest.
articles.summary: Humorous reprint from the Northwest about a cowboy in a sleeping car.

articles.text: G. D. Kennedy returned from his eastern trip Friday evening.
articles.summary: G. D. Kennedy returned from his eastern trip Friday evening.

articles.text: J. W. Allen, Superintendent of the stage line, came in Wednesday.
articles.summary: J. W. Allen, superintendent of the stage line, came in Wednesday.

articles.text: Dr. Jorgens left Monday morning for Spearfish, where he has business interests to look after.
articles.summary: Dr. Jorgens left Monday for business in Spearfish.

articles.text: Vic Smith and his brother Frank came in Saturday night from Bismarck. They will make Medora their home.
articles.summary: Vic Smith and his brother Frank arrived Saturday night from Bismarck to live in Medora.

articles.text: Several improvements have been made in the Co's. offices and the P. O. boxes used in the rink have been put up in the present quarters of the office.
articles.summary: Improvements were made in the Co.'s offices, where the post-office boxes from the rink have been put up.

articles.text: Bob Roberts returned from North Wales last Saturday. He stopped off in New York for several days and reports Jones & Pennell's contract as being a first-rate one.
articles.summary: Bob Roberts returned from North Wales last Saturday, reporting Jones & Pennell's contract a good one.

articles.text: A larger number was in attendance at the rink last Thursday night and there was better music than at any time before in Medora's history. Every one attending was perfectly satisfied.
articles.summary: A larger crowd and better music at the rink last Thursday night.

articles.text: A dance was given at the residence of Mr. Graham in Mingusville by the Misses Graham, last Monday evening. A very pleasant time was had and Mingusville kept up her reputation as a getter-up of pleasant social gatherings.
articles.summary: The Misses Graham gave a dance at Mr. Graham's residence in Mingusville last Monday evening.

articles.text: Revs. Schaffner and Huntley came down Sunday evening and the largest congregation yet assembled here, listened to an interesting sermon from the latter who has charge of north Dakota missions. We hope to see as good a turnout next Sunday evening when Mr. Schaffner will again be here.
articles.summary: Revs. Schaffner and Huntley came down Sunday; Huntley preached to the largest congregation yet; Schaffner will preach next Sunday.

articles.text: The N. P. R. C. Co. expect by next year to handle at least 500 cattle a day. About half of these will be shipped alive. From figures furnished us by the Marquis it appears that on this number of cattle, over $250,000 will be saved during the season by adopting the lake route via Duluth to Buffalo and thence to New York.
articles.summary: The N. P. R. C. Co. expects to handle 500 cattle a day next year and save over $250,000 using the lake route via Duluth, per figures from the Marquis.

articles.text: The St Paul Globe, with its usual correctness, states that Theodore Roosevelt passed through St. Paul lately on his way to his ranch on the Elkhorn. For the benefit of the Globe's thick-witted stock editor we would state that the name Elkhorn applies to the brand on the cattle and not to any river, creek, coulie, ravine or butte in the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: The paper ridicules the St. Paul Globe for saying Theodore Roosevelt passed through St. Paul to his ranch "on the Elkhorn," explaining Elkhorn is a brand.

articles.text: The rink shooting contests have been decided, A. T. Packard winning the one offered to members of the gun club and Mose Ryder the one offered to those not members. Packard's score averaged fifty-three and three-twentieths out of a possible sixty and Ryder's averaged fifty-one. The range was seventy-five feet, the bulls eye being an inch and a half. The best score was five straight bull's eyes, made by Packard.
articles.summary: A. T. Packard won the gun-club rink shooting contest and Mose Ryder the non-members' contest.

articles.text: The Marquis is enthusiastic over the fact that the streak of whitish clay found about twenty feet above the largest lignite veins near here has turned out to be kaoline. This is the finest kind of pottery clay, the most costly ware being made from it. If it turns out as expected the Marquis will put up large works, which will draw more money to Medora than the slaughtering business. We certainly hope there will be no disappointment in this new discovery.
articles.summary: The Marquis is enthusiastic over kaolin clay found above lignite veins near Medora and may build pottery works.

articles.text: The Medora branch of the Boston clothing, boot and shoe store opened up in good shape last Friday. Their goods are of first-class quality and prices are scarcely higher than those quoted in St. Paul. The Co. now has branches at Dayton, Ohio, Bismarck, Mandan and Medora, Dak., and Miles City, Billings and Glendive, Montana. They own a factory at 631 Broadway N. Y. and are thus able to undersell any firm in the west. The establishment of a branch here is gladly welcomed and will be liberally patronized. The resident manager T. W. Gordon has already made a good impression here and we see no reason why the store should not do a large business.
articles.summary: The Medora branch of the Boston clothing, boot and shoe store opened last Friday under resident manager T. W. Gordon.

articles.text: The Willard Bros., after selling a few horses here and allowing the bunch to recruit up started for the Hills, where the most of the band has been contracted. Cap., Fred and Ed. Turner made many friends here and if they will quit rustling we would be glad to see them again. We regret exceedingly, though, that Cap. should have wasted so much raw material as to have picked such places to pound holes in the ground off his bucking cayuse as can never be used even for post holes. Fred said that he never was so sorry for anything in his life as to see Cap. thrown but—well, we all know Fred. We might add that Fisher intends getting out a writ of habeas-corpus to recover the coat Cap. rustled.
articles.summary: The Willard Bros. sold horses and left for the Black Hills; the paper jokes about Cap. Turner being thrown and a coat "rustled."

articles.text: All members of the order of A., F. & A. M., in good standing, are requested to meet at the rink on Friday evening this week, after the firemen's meeting, to consider the advisability of establishing a lodge at this place.
articles.summary: Masons are asked to meet at the rink Friday evening to consider establishing a lodge.

articles.text: Fifteen hundred head of states yearlings and two's came in Tuesday morning for the Elkhorn and Chimney Butte ranches of Theodore Roosevelt. They were in fair condition after their long ride and except for the disadvantage of a large number being yearlings, give every evidence of growing into good beef. The larger majority are steers. A good lot of Short-horn bulls and one Polled-Angus were in the herd. A thousand of these cattle will be driven to the Elkhorn ranch and five hundred to the already well-stocked Chimney Butte ranch.
articles.summary: 1,500 head of yearlings and two-year-olds arrived Tuesday for Theodore Roosevelt's Elkhorn and Chimney Butte ranches.

articles.text: There will be a meeting to-morrow night at the rink which every man having a cents worth of interest in Medora or Little Missouri, should feel it his duty to attend. Several points of interest will be brought up, the first of which is fire protection. As good a bucket brigade as possible will be formed which will be able to do much good in case of fire. A movement will also be set on foot to organize a regular school, which will receive the consideration of the meeting. A third point will be to organize in such a way that in case of any lawlessness or the desirability of "firing stiffs" we can have men to depend on in doing the work. Another point to be brought up is that of grading and otherwise improving the streets. Bob Roberts has proved beyond doubt that scoria, when beaten down and mixed with the clay and sand makes a first-rate macadam. There is enough scoria here to pave a city and means will be found to utilize it. The meeting will be held at 7:30 and we hope to see every one interested present.
articles.summary: A town meeting at the rink to-morrow night will take up fire protection, a school, law and order, and street grading with scoria.

articles.text: Having read the private diary kept by Vic Smith on his trip from Poplar river to Bismarck by boat in search of beaver, we are only sorry that we cannot publish it in full. He started from Medora March 4th and reached Glendive in time to see a "Democratic twenty-years' drunk." Starting from Glendive for Poplar creek in a buckboard stage(?) he had one drunken driver after another until the climax was capped by one jehu trying to pull to pieces a bedstead with a good Indian on it. As Vic had too great a respect for his scalp to meddle with dead Indians he induced the driver to go on. At Wolf Point about 200 government cattle had died and the Indians were having a glorious time. At Ft. Galpin, on the Missouri, he got a team to take him to Milk river, camping in the deserted shack of Tom Cambell, a man who kept forty-seven diffierent squaws. He became wringing wet from breaking into streams and for some time had to live on sage hens and prairie dogs. At Milk river he camped awaiting the spring break-up. One day shooting a goose, it fell on a gorge and just as he had secured it with the aid of a long pole, the gorge broke and he had a parrot and monkey time getting on shore. When he did return, he found that the Indians had stolen all his grub. Here in his diary he remarked that he observed the fourth commandment. The day was Sunday and we are left in a state of harrowing uncertainly as to whether he meant the fourth or fifth. Here he killed several beaver and on March 26th the river broke and he started down stream in his skiff. After a number of dangerous experiences he landed in Bismack with about $300 worth of beaver skins.
articles.summary: Vic Smith's diary of his March trip from Medora via Glendive and Milk river down the Missouri to Bismarck trapping beaver.
